title: Break It Down, Pass It On: Cross-Task Skill Transfer in LLM Agents

visual_explainer.blocker: No paper-grounded mechanism figure was available; the record remains text-only rather than publishing an unverified synthesis.

analysis.tldr: Persistent skills distilled per subtask transfer more reliably than whole-task skills on average, while whole-task text and code memories can reduce success. The evidence supports granularity as a consumer-dependent policy, not a universal subtask advantage.
analysis.problem: A skill written from an entire trajectory can bind incidental task details; finer subtask units may transfer better, but also increase writes, retrieval calls, and path dependence.
analysis.core_idea: Induce text or executable-code skills after each task or subtask, retrieve top-5 descriptions on later distinct tasks, inject or load them into the actor, and compare matched no-memory variants across three agent environments.

memory_design.write: One LLM call turns each completed task or subtask trajectory into a persistent text workflow or Python function.
memory_design.organize: Descriptions drive embedding retrieval; text may merge, code may overwrite/deduplicate, and unloadable code triggers cascading dependent pruning.
memory_design.read: Task agents query once and subtask agents query per subtask; top-5 skills enter context and code functions enter the execution namespace.
memory_design.update_forget: Condition-specific libraries evolve from earlier behavior, with merge, overwrite, deduplication, and failure-driven pruning.

compared_to: Task-level text/code memory versus the same task agent without memory
Subtask-level text/code memory versus the same subtask agent without memory
A frozen subtask library replayed into the task actor for a consumer-matched granularity check
analysis.evidence: Across 11 models and 809 tasks, task no-memory is 22.1%, Task+Text 20.9%, and Task+Code 18.0%; subtask no-memory is 24.8%, Subtask+Text 26.7%, and Subtask+Code 25.3%. A two-model frozen-library replay reports task actors using subtask skills +9.9pp on average, but primary confidence intervals overlap and many model/domain slices reverse.
analysis.why_it_matters: Procedural memory needs a write-unit policy matched to the later consumer; more elaborate or executable artifacts are not automatically more reusable.
limitations: Task and subtask agents differ in planner, summarizer, query frequency, write count, and condition-specific source trajectories; format also changes execution affordance.
No task-order randomization, replicated seeds, or paired primary test is reported; the claimed repository contains no code or data when verified.
Induction, embeddings, context injection, dependency loading, merge/prune, tokens, dollars, storage, and energy are not fully accounted.
